property_summary: The reference contract forbids transferring ownership to the zero address (transferOwnership(address(0)) always reverts), whereas the mutant removes that check allowing owner to become address(0); the test asserts that calling transferOwnership with a fuzzed newOwner either reverts (when newOwner == address(0)) or sets owner to newOwner (for non-zero), and thus the reference never ends up with owner == address(0) while the mutant can.

For every address newOwner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the reference either reverts when newOwner == address(0) or results in owner() == newOwner for non-zero; the mutant allows owner() to become address(0) (i.e. the reference never ends with owner() == address(0) after a successful call but the mutant can), so asserting that either the call reverted or owner() != address(0) holds for all inputs on the reference and is violated by the mutant for some input.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the reference either reverts if newOwner == address(0) or results in owner() == newOwner; equivalently, after a successful transferOwnership call on the reference, owner() is never address(0) — the mutant can set owner() to address(0) for some inputs, violating this invariant.

For any caller, transferOwnership can only be successfully invoked by the owner when the contract checks msg.sender (reference); the mutant that additionally compares owner() to tx.origin allows a non-owner contract (a caller through a contract) to pass the tx.origin check and thus lets a non-owner contract transfer ownership, violating the rule for some inputs.

For all callers and call contexts, only the current owner (owner() == msg.sender) can successfully call transferOwnership; the mutant that additionally checks tx.origin allows a non-owner contract caller (where tx.origin is the EOA owner but msg.sender is a contract) to succeed, violating this property for some inputs.
